topics: 🍎 Same Courtyard or a Different One? — Rava's dilemma about bringing a fruit-filled hand back
🔥 Bread Stuck to the Oven — the long road to understanding Rav Beivai bar Abaye's dilemma
📏 Does Placing Need a 4×4 Space? — why the poor person is liable despite his tiny hand
🌀 Caught in the Air Is Like Placed — Rabbi Akiva's doctrine of קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה
🌳 A Different Source? — Rav Yosef reattributes the mishna to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Fruit, Bread, and the Size of a 'Place'
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 4a–4b
overview.hebrewSource: יָדוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם חֲשׁוּבָה לוֹ כְּאַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing from the previous daf's discussion of a fruit-filled hand, Rava asks Rav Nachman a sharper question: does it matter whether he returns his hand to the same courtyard or a different one? The Gemara then works through Rav Beivai bar Abaye's dilemma about bread stuck to an oven wall — testing whether it describes an unwitting or intentional violator, and whether the Sages would ever permit breaking one prohibition to avoid a worse one. The daf's second half turns to a technical question: the mishna requires that lifting and placing occur over an area of four by four handbreadths, yet the poor person's tiny hand is nowhere near that size. The Gemara resolves this through Rabbi Akiva's principle that an object caught in mid-air is considered as if it were placed, then explores whether the mishna might instead reflect Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's opinion.

slides.title: 🍎 Same Courtyard, Different Courtyard
slides.subtitle: Rava's follow-up dilemma to Rav Nachman
rows: Back to the SAME courtyard he stood in
His original plan — to move the fruit elsewhere — was never achieved; requiring him to bring it back is itself a kind of penalty
His original plan WAS achieved — he actually relocated the fruit, so the Sages forbid completing the transfer there

callout.label: Rav Nachman's quip:
callout.text: When Rava pressed for the logic behind the distinction, Rav Nachman answered wryly, 'By the time you finish eating a kor of salt over it, you'll understand' — before giving the real answer above.

slides.title: 🔥 Bread Stuck to the Oven
slides.subtitle: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's dilemma, worked out step by step

steps.content: 1️⃣ Dilemma: one who stuck bread to the wall of a heated oven on Shabbat — may he remove it before it fully bakes, to avoid liability?
2️⃣ If he remains unaware of his error, no one could ever ask this question — so he must have later remembered

3️⃣ But if he remembered while it was still baking, a known rule exempts him already (liability requires unwitting action from start to finish) — so the case must involve someone who acted intentionally
4️⃣ Rav Sheila proposed instead: still unwitting, but the dilemma is whether others may remove it for him — Rav Sheshet objected: do we tell a person to sin so his friend can benefit?
5️⃣ Rav Ashi's resolution: the man acted intentionally, and the real question is whether he may remove the bread before he becomes liable to stoning — the Sages permitted it

callout.label: Rav Acha's version:
callout.text: Rav Acha, son of Rava, taught this not as an open dilemma but as a settled ruling: one who stuck bread to the oven may remove it before incurring liability to stoning.

slides.title: 📏 Why Is the Poor Person Liable With Such a Small Hand?
slides.subtitle: Lifting and placing normally require a surface of four by four handbreadths

nodes.content: ❓ A valid act of lifting or placing needs a surface of four by four handbreadths — but a hand is far smaller. Why is the poor person liable in the mishna at all?
💡 Rabba: this mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that placing does NOT require an area of four by four handbreadths
📜 Source: one who throws an object from a private domain, through the public domain, to another private domain

columns.label: Rabbi Akiva: liable
columns.content: קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה — an object caught in a domain's airspace is considered as if placed there, even without a 4×4 surface

columns.label: The Rabbis: exempt
columns.content: The object merely passed through and never truly came to rest — no valid placing occurred

nodes.content: ✅ Since Rabbi Akiva needs no defined surface for placing, even a hand can serve as a valid place of placing

callout.label: Term:
callout.text: קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה — 'caught [in the air] is as if it had been placed.'

slides.title: 🌳 Whose Opinion Is It, Really?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yosef proposes a different source than Rabbi Akiva

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Even granting Rabbi Akiva's principle — that shows only that placing needs no 4×4 space. Perhaps lifting still requires it!

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef
lines.text: Rather — whose opinion is the mishna following? It is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Which ruling of his? The one where an object lands on a projection (זִיז) of any size, and he deems the thrower liable?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: No — that baraita is a special case: a tree in the private domain whose branches lean into the public domain. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds 'cast its boughs after its trunk' — the branch counts as the private-domain trunk itself.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Rather, it must be this ruling: one who throws from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds him liable twice, once for carrying in and once for carrying out!

callout.label: Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name:
callout.text: Since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi imposes two separate liabilities on that single throw, neither the lifting nor the placing in his view requires an area of four by four handbreadths.

slides.title: 🔍 Two Candidate Sources for 'No 4×4 Required'
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests, and rejects, one ruling of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi before settling on another

boxes.title: Rabbi Akiva
items: קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה — airspace counts as placed

boxes.title: Rejected: the Tree Branch
items: Object lands on a branch leaning into the public domain
Explained instead by 'cast its boughs after its trunk'

boxes.title: Accepted: Double Liability
items: Public → private (middle) → public domain, one throw
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: liable twice, for carrying in AND out
Proves neither lifting nor placing needs a defined area

callout.label: Still open:
callout.text: The Gemara is about to test whether Rav and Shmuel actually agree with this reading of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position.

summary.principle: A fruit-filled hand may return to the same courtyard but not a different one, since only the latter completes the intended transfer; and the mishna's liability for a hand too small to be four by four handbreadths follows either Rabbi Akiva's rule that an object caught in mid-air counts as placed, or Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling that a throw across a middle domain incurs liability twice over.

flowSteps.content: 🍎 Rava to Rav Nachman: hand returned to the SAME courtyard is permitted; to a DIFFERENT courtyard, prohibited
🔥 Rav Beivai bar Abaye's oven dilemma resolved: an intentional violator may remove stuck bread before liability to stoning
📏 Why is a hand — far smaller than 4×4 handbreadths — a valid place of placing?

columns.content: 🌀 Rabbi Akiva: קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה — caught in the air counts as placed
🌳 Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rav Yosef's reading): double liability proves neither lifting nor placing needs a defined area

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the size requirement of four by four handbreadths is not universal — specific tannaim dispense with it for placing, or for both lifting and placing

quiz.q: According to Rav Nachman, why is it permitted to bring a fruit-filled hand back to the SAME courtyard, but prohibited to bring it to a DIFFERENT courtyard?
o: Because different courtyards belong to different owners
Because in the first case his original plan was never achieved, while in the second it was
Because fruit spoils faster in a different courtyard
There is no real difference between the two cases
quiz.e: Returning to the same courtyard undoes an unrealized plan (itself a penalty); moving to a different courtyard completes the very transfer he intended, so it is prohibited.

quiz.q: In Rav Ashi's final understanding of Rav Beivai bar Abaye's dilemma, what was the status of the person who stuck bread to the oven?
o: He acted unwittingly and never learned of his error
He acted intentionally, and the question is whether he may remove it before becoming liable to stoning
He was a priest performing a Temple service
He was exempt because it was before Shabbat began
quiz.e: Rav Ashi (and Rav Acha's explicit version) understood the case as intentional, with the dilemma being whether the Sages permit removing the bread to avoid the far graver punishment of stoning.

quiz.q: Why is the poor person in the mishna liable for placing an object into the homeowner's hand, even though a hand is far smaller than the required four by four handbreadths?
o: Because hands are exempt from the size requirement by Torah law
Because Rabba attributes the mishna to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that an object caught in the air counts as placed without needing a defined surface
Because the homeowner's hand was resting on a table
Because the object weighed less than an olive's bulk
quiz.e: Rabba explains that the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva's principle of קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה — an object caught in a domain's airspace is treated as placed, even without a 4×4 surface.

quiz.q: What does the phrase קְלוּטָה כְּמִי שֶׁהוּנְּחָה mean?
o: An object that is stolen is considered returned
An object caught in the airspace of a domain is considered as if it had been placed there
A hand is always considered a private domain
Bread that is baked is considered eaten
quiz.e: It is Rabbi Akiva's principle that mere passage through, or arrival in, a domain's airspace counts as a completed act of placing.

quiz.q: Which ruling of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does Rav Yosef ultimately use to argue that neither lifting nor placing requires a four by four space?
o: His ruling about the tree whose branches lean into the public domain
His ruling that one who throws from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between is liable twice, for carrying in and carrying out
His ruling about the evening Shema
His ruling about a barrel in the public domain
quiz.e: Because Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi imposes two separate liabilities on a single throw across an intervening private domain, neither the lifting nor the placing in his view can require a defined area.
